title: Untethered intervention at a target inside the living human body

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an internal therapeutic instrument that travels without a physical tether to a chosen target inside a living human, performs a specified treatment, and is then retrieved or safely resorbed. A clinician could guide it through vessels or tissue using external imaging and electromagnetic fields. Proposed actions include releasing a drug, disrupting a clot, or performing a small mechanical intervention; these are examples of the intended capability, not human treatments established by the supplied evidence.

The defining advance is the combination of targeted navigation, therapeutic action, and safe clearance in a human. It does not require the device to carry its own power source, navigation intelligence, or medical judgment. A release catheter can introduce an untethered device, as in the platform described by Landers and colleagues; the proposed milestone concerns its subsequent operation at the treatment target. Navigation alone and onboard computation alone establish useful components, but neither establishes this complete clinical capability.

significance.text: A successful demonstration would establish a new way to perform a targeted internal intervention for the particular anatomy and therapeutic action tested. Targeted drug delivery provides a concrete rationale: concentrating treatment at a diseased site could reduce systemic exposure. Landers and colleagues describe this rationale and a magnetically guided delivery platform, but their retained abstract does not establish human efficacy or comparative clinical benefit.

Conditional significance assessment: an untethered instrument could reduce the need for a catheter to physically reach the final treatment site. If it could reach otherwise difficult targets and perform useful treatment safely, it might expand minimally invasive options or reduce the need for open surgery in selected cases. These are downstream possibilities requiring comparative evidence about access, treatment outcomes, complications, and procedural burden. A successful navigation-and-treatment demonstration would not establish them automatically.

The impact would remain bounded by the demonstrated route, target, payload, and action. One local intervention would not establish general cancer treatment, access to every organ, or autonomous medical judgment. Microscopic programmed autonomy is already reported by Lassiter and colleagues, including behavior changes in response to surroundings. Clinically capable judgment is a distinct requirement, and externally guided treatment could satisfy this concept without it. The supplied evidence also does not justify a blanket comparison portraying existing catheters, endoscopes, or capsules as exclusively passive or limited to imaging.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed remaining milestone is an integrated human demonstration: reach a chosen internal target while untethered, perform a therapeutic action, and establish clearance with defined safety follow-up. The supplied abstracts document relevant technical progress but do not report that complete sequence in humans. They also cannot establish that the milestone remains globally unmet as of November 1, 2026; the supplied review contains no adequate field-wide freshness assessment.

Engineering synthesis: the central difficulty is satisfying several constraints together. A device must fit its intended route while retaining adequate therapeutic payload and actuation capability. Its position must remain visible enough for control, and propulsion or magnetic steering must work under the conditions of the selected anatomy. Movement against blood flow matters where a route requires upstream travel; it is not a universal requirement for every possible in-body intervention. Vessel navigation and movement through tissue would pose different access and control problems.

Engineering synthesis: treatment also requires biocompatible materials, reliable payload retention and release, sufficient precision to avoid unintended action, and a credible retrieval or resorption pathway. A dissolvable capsule is a relevant platform component, but its presence alone does not demonstrate clearance of every device component or establish human safety. These are proposed integration requirements, not a claim that the supplied abstracts experimentally identify every listed barrier as unsolved.

current_state.text: Fabian C. Landers and colleagues’ November 2025 Science paper, “Clinically ready magnetic microrobots for targeted therapies,” reports a platform integrating a clinical electromagnetic navigation system, a custom release catheter, and a dissolvable capsule. Its retained PubMed abstract reports in vitro navigation in human vasculature models, fluoroscopic tracking, and successful navigation in large animal models. These are relevant demonstrations of integrated delivery and navigation technology; human vasculature models are not living human subjects. Despite the paper’s title, the retained abstract does not report completed human therapeutic intervention or human clearance.

Interpretation of the Landers result is limited to the retained abstract. The research notes describe an editor’s summary and a full-article access refusal, but neither is present in the retained material assessed by the review. Consequently, neither the editor’s summary nor the reported access response provides an additional evidentiary basis here. Full-article experimental details and broader clinical conclusions cannot be inferred from this abstract-level record.

The research notes identify a later Science Robotics paper, “AI-driven actuation-compatible tracking for closed-loop navigation of miniature robots in vivo,” dated September 23, 2026. Those notes attribute closed-loop navigation of millimeter-scale magnetic robots in vivo to its abstract. However, the source index contains no retained artifact for that paper, and the review could not assess its text or experimental claims. The reported navigation result therefore remains unverified within this record. This limitation does not show that the result is false, and the notes do not establish human therapeutic action or clearance.

Maya M. Lassiter and colleagues’ December 2025 Science Robotics paper, “Microscopic robots that sense, think, act, and compute,” reports a robot comparable in size to a single-celled paramecium, with onboard computation, sensing, memory, locomotion, and communication. The retained abstract describes execution of digitally defined algorithms and autonomous changes in behavior in response to surroundings. These are demonstrated microscopic control capabilities. The abstract’s prospect of general-purpose microrobots operating without supervision is a forward-looking possibility, and the abstract does not establish autonomous medical judgment, human therapeutic intervention, or clearance. It also does not justify assigning the experiments a particular inside- or outside-the-body setting.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established consensus standard: in a living human, an untethered device reaches a pre-specified anatomical target through vessels or tissue, performs one pre-registered therapeutic action, and is retrieved or shown to resorb. External clinical imaging and electromagnetic guidance are allowed. The protocol should distinguish successful arrival from successful treatment and specify evidence that the action occurred at the intended site.
completion_criteria.label: Living-human untethered treatment at pre-specified target with retrieval or resorption

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and clearance assessment: pre-specified monitoring and follow-up should evaluate device clearance and device-attributable injury, with successful completion requiring no detected new injury attributable to the device during the defined interval. Retrieval should account for the introduced device, while a resorption claim should account for relevant components and their fate. No particular follow-up duration or numerical safety threshold is supplied here. Absence of detected injury would support safety only within the sensitivity, duration, and circumstances of that assessment.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-specified follow-up detects no new device-attributable injury with accounted clearance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: convincing evidence should include repeatable targeting, therapeutic action, and clearance across reported attempts, transparent reporting of failures and adverse events, and replication sufficient to distinguish a reproducible capability from an isolated success. Reports should specify anatomy, device dimensions, payload, guidance and imaging requirements, route, and operating conditions. A vasculature phantom, animal navigation alone, a capsule used only for imaging, or a programmable robot in a dish would not satisfy the proposed human therapeutic milestone. Even repeated human successes would establish demonstrated breadth for tested circumstances, not universal access, unrestricted safety, or superiority to existing care.
completion_criteria.label: Repeatable human attempts with failures and operating conditions reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ROB-10, “Completion of full surgical procedures on living patients,” is the closest clinical neighbor. ROB-06 concerns a targeted therapeutic action by an untethered device and allows external clinician guidance. ROB-10 concerns completion of a whole surgical procedure. An untethered instrument could eventually contribute to such a procedure, but one successful local treatment would not establish full-procedure completion, and a completed procedure would not necessarily involve an untethered device.

Roster-based synthesis: ROB-01, “Reliable instruction-following physical work in unfamiliar everyday environments,” and ROB-09, “Lifelong on-robot learning that retains and composes physical skills,” concern broader behavioral capabilities. ROB-06 could succeed with a tightly specified intervention and external control, without general instruction following or lifelong learning. Lassiter’s microscopic programmed autonomy is a relevant enabling direction, but the reported capabilities do not establish either roster milestone or human therapeutic intervention.

Roster-based synthesis: ROB-02, “Autonomous dexterous tool use and in-hand manipulation at human reliability,” overlaps with the precision needed for mechanical treatment, while ROB-07, “Predictive contact mechanics that plans real manipulation,” could contribute to planning device–tissue interactions. Neither is required by every version of ROB-06: guided local drug release could satisfy the proposed milestone without general dexterous tool use or a general predictive contact model.

Roster-based synthesis: ROB-03, “An artificial muscle that can serve as the main actuator of a useful robot,” concerns an actuation technology rather than a clinical endpoint. Such an actuator could be useful in a future internal instrument, but the supplied Landers platform uses electromagnetic guidance. ROB-06 therefore does not depend on achieving artificial-muscle actuation, and an artificial-muscle demonstration would not establish in-body treatment or clearance.

Roster-based synthesis: ROB-04, “Closed-loop robotic self-reproduction from feedstock,” ROB-05, “Load-bearing robotic matter that reforms into working machines,” and ROB-08, “Robot collectives that build functional structures from bulk material,” address reproduction, reconfiguration, and collective construction. A future therapeutic system might draw on reconfiguration or coordinated devices, but ROB-06 requires none of those capabilities. Conversely, self-reproduction, shape change, or collective construction would not demonstrate targeted human therapy and safe clearance.

change_log.change: Preserved ROB-06’s identity and integrated navigation, therapeutic action, and clearance into a single human milestone.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent even though the supplied evidence does not establish its present-day global absence.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims that the breakthrough remains unmet with a bounded statement about what the supplied abstracts report.
change_log.reason: The review lacks a sufficient freshness assessment to establish field-wide status as of November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Retained the joint engineering constraints as explicitly labeled synthesis and made propulsion against blood flow route-dependent.
change_log.reason: The abstracts do not substantiate the entire barrier list or make upstream propulsion necessary for every intervention.

change_log.change: Preserved the dated Landers navigation and platform results while limiting their interpretation to the retained abstract.
change_log.reason: The review supports model and large-animal navigation but cannot verify the claimed editor’s summary, access response, or full-article details.

change_log.change: Retained the September 2026 tracking paper as an explicitly unverified report from the research notes.
change_log.reason: Omitting it entirely would lose potentially useful research context, but no retained artifact supports treating its experimental claims as assessed findings.

change_log.change: Distinguished demonstrated microscopic programmed autonomy from autonomous medical judgment.
change_log.reason: Lassiter’s abstract supports onboard computation and responsive behavior, so a blanket assertion that onboard autonomy is wholly missing would be misleading.

change_log.change: Removed unsupported generalizations about existing internal instruments and treated reduced surgery as a conditional downstream benefit.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence establishes neither those categorical comparisons nor comparative clinical outcomes.

change_log.change: Specified therapeutic action, defined follow-up, clearance assessment, reproducibility, and bounded interpretation in the proposed completion criteria.
change_log.reason: These changes make the proposal assessable without presenting an invented consensus standard or equating no detected injury with unrestricted safety.

change_log.change: Explained overlap and distinctions with every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Related enabling capabilities and broader clinical milestones should remain separate concepts.

unresolved_issues: Whether any system had completed the proposed human intervention-and-clearance milestone by November 1, 2026 remains unresolved by the supplied evidence.
The September 2026 tracking paper has no retained source artifact; its reported experimental scope, millimeter-scale dimensions, and outcomes cannot be assessed here.
The supplied research gives the tracking paper’s article identifier as eae0592 while its supplied DOI ends in aee0592. That bibliographic discrepancy remains unresolved.
Full-article details for the two 2025 papers are unavailable in the reviewed evidence, limiting assessment of experimental conditions, performance, failure modes, and safety.
Suitable anatomy, therapeutic action, device dimensions, clearance evidence, follow-up duration, and replication requirements remain to be specified for an actual demonstration.
Comparative evidence would be needed to establish reduced systemic exposure, reduced surgical burden, improved outcomes, or practical advantages for a particular human application.

The review’s recommendation to remove the September 2026 experimental claim was adopted for established findings but not as complete omission: the report is preserved solely as an unverified research attribution so its uncertainty and potential relevance remain visible.

brief.title: Targeted treatment by tiny devices inside the body
possible: A patient could receive treatment from a tiny device that travels through blood vessels or tissue without a physical tether. It would reach a chosen site, release a drug or perform a small mechanical treatment, then be removed or safely broken down by the body. A clinician could guide it using medical imaging and magnetic fields.
why: Delivering a drug directly to diseased tissue could concentrate treatment where it is needed and reduce exposure elsewhere in the body.
Reaching difficult internal targets could expand treatment options through small openings and reduce the need for open surgery in selected cases.

sources.showed: They built a magnetically guided drug-delivery platform with a release tube and a dissolvable capsule. They demonstrated navigation in models of human blood vessels and in large animals, with X-ray tracking.
sources.quote: in vivo experiments confirmed tracking under fluoroscopy and successful navigation in large animal models.
sources.cited_for: This work supports guided delivery and navigation under conditions relevant to treatment inside the body.
sources.not_established: Human treatment at a chosen target and safe clearance of all device components remain to be demonstrated.

sources.showed: This study concerns computer-guided tracking that feeds position measurements back into control of miniature robots inside living bodies.
sources.cited_for: The study concerns tracking and guidance during movement inside the body.
sources.not_established: Human therapeutic action and safe device clearance remain to be demonstrated.

sources.showed: They built microscopic robots with onboard computing, sensing, memory, movement and communication. The robots executed programmed rules and changed their behavior in response to their surroundings.
sources.quote: Built massively in parallel with fully lithographic processing, these microrobots can execute digitally defined algorithms and autonomously change behavior in response to their surroundings.
sources.cited_for: This work establishes that microscopic robots can carry computing and responsive control onboard.
sources.not_established: Human treatment, safe device clearance and medical judgment remain to be demonstrated.

shown: Landers and colleagues have combined magnetic guidance, a release tube and a dissolvable capsule in a drug-delivery platform. They demonstrated navigation in large animals. Lassiter and colleagues have separately demonstrated microscopic robots that run programs and respond to their surroundings.
missing: A human demonstration must combine arrival at a chosen internal target, treatment there and removal or safe breakdown of the device.
Follow-up must account for the device’s components and assess injury attributable to them.
Repeated human attempts must establish reliability, including failures and the conditions in which treatment works.

milestones.label: Human treatment at a chosen site with device clearance
milestones.explanation: A device would have to reach a preselected target in a living human without a tether, perform the planned treatment, and be removed or safely broken down. This would establish the complete treatment sequence.

milestones.label: Follow-up finds no device injury and accounts for clearance
milestones.explanation: Planned follow-up would have to account for the device and its components and detect no new injury attributable to it. This would support safety within the monitoring period and its ability to detect harm.

milestones.label: Repeated human successes with failures and conditions reported
milestones.explanation: Human attempts would have to repeat targeting, treatment and clearance, with failures, adverse events and operating conditions reported. Replication would establish reliability and the circumstances in which the capability works.

uncertain: The anatomy, treatment, device size and guidance requirements suitable for a human demonstration remain open.
The necessary follow-up duration, sensitivity of injury detection and extent of replication remain to be defined.
Whether a particular treatment would reduce drug exposure elsewhere, surgical burden or complications requires comparison with existing care.

page.title: Untethered robotic intervention in humans
page.definition: An untethered miniature robot navigates to a specified site inside a living human, performs a therapeutic action there, and is retrieved or undergoes demonstrated biocompatible breakdown and clearance. Untethered means no physical connection remains during navigation and treatment; external power, imaging and clinician control are permitted.

goal.need: ARPA-H reports that only 12% of 335,000 eligible U.S. stroke patients receive thrombectomy, the removal of a blood clot, each year. Its AIR programme funds an untethered clot-removal robot as one response to this treatment-access gap.

rows: Americans living over one hour from a thrombectomy hospital
figures.note: Programme rationale; these figures do not measure microrobot treatment outcomes.

completion.title: An untethered robot treats a specified internal target in a human and completes clearance follow-up.
completion.criterion: In at least one living human, the same untethered robot reaches a specified internal target, performs the intended therapeutic action there, and is retrieved or shown to undergo biocompatible breakdown and clearance. The clinical protocol specifies evidence of targeting and treatment, the fate of every component, device-related safety endpoints and follow-up duration; the case meets those endpoints. External power, imaging and clinician guidance are allowed. No universal success rate or follow-up interval is imposed.
completion.set_by: Atlas; provisional human demonstration criterion extending the published programme and clinical-development goals.
completion.basis: Searched FDA feasibility guidance, AIR TA2 criteria, microrobotics roadmaps, ISO catalogue descriptions and indexed trial records; no published human test combining targeting, treatment and complete clearance was located. AIR specifies an animal test; FDA describes initial human safety and functionality studies. One documented human intervention meeting its protocol's safety and clearance endpoints is the narrowest extension of those goals.

milestones.title: Microrobots reproduce integrated movement, sensing and treatment in a 3D biological model at least five times.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate integrated movement, sensing and therapeutic action in a biologically relevant 3D in vitro system at least five times. AIR permits cadaver or in vivo substitutes when an in vitro testbed is impractically burdensome and performance can be quantified. Supporting result: Landers et al., 13 November 2025, report reperfusion beginning 7.5 minutes after drug release in a silicone artery model containing a human blood clot; the main article gives no clot-lysis replicate count.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, AIR solicitation Amendment 01, Table 6, Integrated Core Microbot Functions; threshold is tabulated.

milestones.title: Microrobots perform an intervention at a clinically relevant animal target at least five times.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate microrobot action at a clinically relevant target in a small-animal model at least five times; a large animal may substitute when robot size or other characteristics require it. Related component evidence: the institutional abstract of Hu et al., published on 23 September 2026, reports in vivo validation of tracking for closed-loop navigation, without an animal count or therapeutic outcome. That abstract does not establish this intervention threshold.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, AIR solicitation Amendment 01, Table 6, Sensing and Action Demonstration in Small Animal; threshold is tabulated.

milestones.title: Microrobots complete autonomous treatment and exit or disintegration in large animals at least five times.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate autonomous deployment, navigation to the target, intervention, and exit or disintegration in a large animal, accounting for every robot; reproduce the complete sequence at least five times. Related result: Landers et al. report guidance of two microrobots into an ovine fourth ventricle and navigation in porcine blood vessels. Their main article does not report this complete treatment-and-clearance sequence.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, AIR solicitation Amendment 01, Table 6, End-to-end in vivo Performance in Large Animal; threshold is tabulated and requires autonomy.

milestones.title: A human study of an untethered therapeutic robot receives FDA and institutional review board approval.
milestones.criterion: For the U.S. significant-risk device pathway, a first human study has an approved investigational device exemption from FDA and approval from the institutional review board at each participating site, permitting enrollment within the authorized limits. The exemption permits clinical investigation. FDA's early-feasibility framework evaluates initial clinical safety and device functionality; the required evidence and enrollment limits depend on the device and protocol.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, IDE Approval Process, Significant Risk Device and When to Apply sections.
milestones.threshold_quote: require both FDA and an Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval prior to initiation of a clinical study.

not_found: ClinicalTrials.gov searches for microrobot and Bionaut could not be opened; registry status remains unverified.
No published human report satisfying the complete intervention-and-clearance criterion was located.
The September 2026 tracking paper was accessible through its institutional abstract; its full experimental results and animal sample sizes could not be checked.
No publicly verifiable authorization for a device-specific human study satisfying milestone m4 was located.

results.finding: Microrobots navigated human vasculature models in vitro; sample size was not reported.
results.detail: The abstract does not establish integrated sensing and treatment in a biologically relevant 3D model, or at least five repetitions.
results.quote: In vitro tests showed precise navigation in human vasculature models, and in vivo experiments confirmed tracking under fluoroscopy and successful navigation in large animal models.

results.finding: Microrobots were tracked and navigated in large animal models; animal count was not reported.
results.detail: The abstract reports navigation but does not establish an intervention at a clinically relevant animal target, five repetitions, or why a large animal substitute was required.

results.finding: Magnetic microrobot swarms treated breast tumors in mice (n=6 per group), achieving 87.52% tumor growth inhibition.
results.detail: Microrobots were administered near the tumor and magnetically actuated to penetrate it. The reported inhibition is a group-level result; individual responses are not specified in the supplied text.
results.quote: Microrobot swarms actuated at WMF–5 Hz achieved 87.52% tumor growth inhibition, which was higher compared to those at WMF–1 Hz (74.67% tumor growth inhibition).

results.finding: Drug-loaded magnetic nanorobots performed thrombolysis at femoral vein clots in rats; n=5 in the treatment group.
results.detail: Blood perfusion was measured in five rats per group. The paper reports enhanced thrombolysis in the magnetically actuated, drug-loaded nanorobot group; it does not give individual-animal outcomes.
results.quote: The above in vivo thrombolysis results clearly confirm that the swarming t-PA–loaded HPB-NRs can effectively dissolve the thrombus in the femoral vein.

results.finding: In 3 treated sheep, untethered microrobot delivery, magnetic navigation, dwell, and retrieval were completed.
results.detail: The study reports three completed workflows, fewer than the five required. The text does not establish autonomous operation or a therapeutic intervention; disease-specific efficacy remains for future study.
results.quote: The full workflow was completed in all 3 treated animals without conversion or rescue. Cannulation succeeded on the first attempt; continuous fluoroscopic visibility and stable magnetic control were maintained; and retrieval succeeded in a single maneuver.

results.finding: In 5 tumor-bearing mice, magnetically guided CAR-NK microrobot treatment reduced tumor signal to 28.4% of peak.
results.detail: The study reports tumor targeting and treatment in mice, as well as infiltration in 3D tumor spheres. It does not establish five integrated movement, sensing and treatment trials in a qualifying 3D model or substitute.
